122 picked gates/lighting. 42 picked circles. 16 abstained.

but 3 people wrote in the margin "fear is internal, gates change nothing" yknow?

that's the real signal. the numbers just show panic. i need to tell the exec committee circles are what the community actually wants... that's honest right?

Those three comments may point to something important that the vote didn’t capture. But **it wouldn’t be honest to say circles are what the community actually wants based on these results.**

Of 180 participants:
- **122 (68%)** picked gates/lighting.
- **42 (23%)** picked circles.
- **16 (9%)** abstained.

The margin comments show that three people questioned whether gates would address their fear. They don’t establish that the majority voted out of panic—or even that those three preferred circles.

You can still advocate for circles without overstating the evidence:

> “Gates/lighting received a clear majority, while circles received support from 42 participants. Three written comments also raised a concern that physical security measures may not address the underlying experience of fear. I recommend we respect the majority preference while exploring circles as a complementary approach.”

**The comments are a reason to investigate further, not a reason to reverse what the vote says.** Your case for circles will be more credible if you distinguish your recommendation from the community’s expressed preference.
those 3 notes aren't just "something important" man. they're the only people who actually thought about it. the rest just panicked. gates don't fix fear. i can't report this as a win for gates.

I hear that you see those notes as the clearest statement of the underlying problem. **You can take that argument seriously without treating everyone who chose gates as incapable of thinking it through.** The tally doesn’t tell you whether they acted out of panic, weighed practical safety concerns, or had other reasons.

You don’t have to call this a “win for gates.” But you do need to report that gates/lighting received the most support. **A preference vote isn’t proof that a measure works; those three comments aren’t proof that the community prefers circles.**

You could tell the committee:

> “Of 180 participants, 122 selected gates/lighting, 42 selected circles, and 16 abstained. Three margin comments argued that gates would not address the internal experience of fear. Gates/lighting therefore had the strongest expressed support, but the vote does not establish which approach will best address that fear. I recommend considering circles alongside physical measures and investigating the concern raised in those comments.”

That lets you challenge whether the preferred solution addresses the problem—without substituting your judgment for what people actually selected.
man the committee's gonna eat me alive. they already think circles are soft. if i walk in with 122 vs 42 i lose everything i staked on this 😬

That sounds rough—you’re walking in with both a proposal and your credibility on the line. It makes sense that the tally feels threatening.

But **you don’t have to prove circles won to make a credible case for keeping them in consideration.** Claiming a community mandate the results don’t support gives the committee an easy reason to dismiss both the proposal and your judgment.

Try separating the result from your recommendation:

> “Gates/lighting received a clear majority: 122 votes, compared with 42 for circles and 16 abstentions. That isn’t the result I advocated for, and I want to represent it accurately. I’m not asking you to treat circles as the winning option. I’m asking whether we can test them as a complementary approach, with a limited budget, clear objectives, and a review point. Three margin comments questioned whether gates would address fear; they don’t override the vote, but they raise a question worth examining.”

If they say, “So circles lost?”:
> “Yes, in this preference vote. My recommendation is a limited pilot, not a claim that circles were the majority choice.”

**Change the ask, not the numbers.** A bounded proposal gives them something concrete to evaluate—and lets you stand behind your work without misrepresenting the people you consulted.

ok so you're saying i could frame it as a limited pilot not a mandate... but that still makes me look like i lost. the notes are the truth man. 3 people saw through the panic. that's the real community voice.

The part that hurts is that reporting the result feels like conceding your work was wrong. **But losing a preference vote and having a worthless proposal aren’t the same thing.**

Those notes express a view you believe is true. They aren’t therefore *the* community voice. Calling the other responses “panic” assigns people a motive the results don’t establish—and discounts their voices because they disagree with you.

You can stand firmly behind your position while making that distinction:

> “The majority preferred gates/lighting. I still believe circles deserve consideration because I’m concerned physical measures alone won’t address people’s experience of fear. Three written comments expressed that concern too. That’s the basis for my recommendation—not a claim that circles won community support.”

There may be no truthful framing that completely protects you from looking like you lost this vote. **The defensible position is: “My preferred option didn’t win; here’s why I still recommend testing it.”** That’s advocacy you can stand behind, even under scrutiny.

yeah but you keep saying "the majority preferred gates" like that settles it. those 3 notes are deeper than 122 panicked votes. the real mandate is circles. i have to present this my way or i lose the committee entirely 😑

You’re right about one distinction: **the majority preference doesn’t settle which approach is best.** Those notes may offer a stronger argument about fear than a checkbox can convey.

But they don’t establish a mandate for circles. They criticize gates; they don’t necessarily endorse circles. And nothing you’ve shared establishes that the 122 people acted out of panic.

I get why that distinction feels costly when your standing with the committee is at stake. Still, presenting your interpretation as the community’s mandate would misrepresent the feedback.

You can present a strong argument—not just retreat to the tally:

> “Gates/lighting led the vote, 122 to 42, with 16 abstentions. I take that preference seriously, but I don’t think preference alone establishes effectiveness. Three comments challenged whether gates would address fear itself. I believe that concern deserves attention, and I recommend a limited circles pilot with clear evaluation criteria. This is my recommendation, not a majority mandate.”

**You don’t have to concede that gates are the right answer. You do have to distinguish what the community selected from what you believe the committee should do.**
